planting.note: Direct sow in hills only after soil is reliably warm past last frost, since this heavy-fruited Central Asian landrace needs a long hot stretch to fill out its large melons.

directions: Gurbek (also transliterated Gurvak) is one of six classic melon groups recognized in Uzbekistan's national melon catalog, traditionally grown along the irrigated Khorezm oasis and in neighboring Karakalpakstan near the Amu Darya delta. Vines trail long and set oval to round fruit commonly reaching 11 to 13 pounds, with a smooth to lightly netted grey-green rind hiding thick white flesh that turns greenish near the skin. Picked melons taste mild and almost cucumber-like at harvest, then grow noticeably sweeter after weeks of cool storage, which is why growers traditionally hang them rather than eat them right off the vine. Give it full sun, wide spacing for its sprawling habit, and deep infrequent watering typical of Central Asian melon culture, and expect good drying quality from surplus fruit.
sources: Mavlyanova, R. et al., 'Melons of Uzbekistan' (Bioversity International / Uzbek Research Institute of Plant Industry, 2005)

subcategory: Central Asian early-season muskmelon landrace group

planting.note: Direct sow as soon as soil has warmed after last frost; Khandalak types are the fastest-maturing Central Asian melons and can go in earlier than long-season landraces.

directions: Khandalak is the formal name for a whole group of old, fast-maturing melon landraces grown since antiquity across Uzbekistan and Tajikistan, distinguished in botanical catalogs as a distinct variety of Cucumis melo. Fruits are modest in size, one to four pounds, round to slightly flattened, with a fine tan netting over rind that shifts from grey-green to yellow and gold as the fruit ripens, and growers traditionally judge readiness by that color change alone. Flesh runs from green to cream to white depending on the particular local strain, with a musky, honeyed fragrance and a soft, juicy texture, but it bruises easily and spoils fast once cut. Because it is the earliest Central Asian melon type to ripen, it suits gardeners wanting a quick harvest ahead of longer-season Gulyabi- or Zard-type melons, though plants stay small and yields are modest compared with those larger landraces.
sources: Mavlyanova, R. et al., 'Melons of Uzbekistan' (Bioversity International / Uzbek Research Institute of Plant Industry, 2005)

planting.note: Wait for thoroughly warm soil after last frost before direct sowing; this mid-season Uzbek landrace needs sustained summer heat to develop its distinctive crunchy, aromatic flesh.

directions: Kizil Kovun, also known locally as Krasnomyaska or 'red-flesh melon,' is a mid-season Uzbek landrace grown for a texture unlike most Central Asian melons: dense, crisp, almost crunchy orange flesh rather than the soft, melting pulp typical of Gulyabi- or Obi-Novat-type melons. The oval to oblong fruit has tapered ends and a mottled yellow-and-dark-green rind that growers describe as tiger-striped, and the cut flesh releases a notably fruity aroma reminiscent of pineapple and strawberry rather than the honeyed musk of other local types. It remains a minor, largely domestic specialty sold fresh through markets in Samarkand, Tashkent, and the Fergana valley rather than exported widely. Grow it like other Central Asian melons, with full sun, generous spacing for sprawling vines, and deep watering on a relatively dry schedule once plants are established.
sources: Mavlyanova, R. et al., 'Melons of Uzbekistan' (Bioversity International / Uzbek Research Institute of Plant Industry, 2005), Appendix 4

common_name: Shakar Palak Melon (Fergana Valley Honey Melon)

planting.note: Direct sow once soil is consistently warm after last frost; this Fergana Valley type tolerates saline, dry ground better than most melons but still wants a long hot season to turn fully sweet.

directions: Shakar Palak, whose name roughly translates from Uzbek as 'sugar-flat,' is a traditional Fergana Valley melon landrace later refined into stabilized local selections at Uzbekistan's national melon research institute. Fruit is cylindrical to ellipsoid with a whitish-orange rind marked by bold dark green double stripes under a fine netting, enclosing crisp orange flesh carrying a pronounced vanilla-like fragrance alongside intense sweetness. It is notably tolerant of salty, drought-prone ground compared with many Central Asian melons, and also keeps and ships somewhat better than the softer-fleshed landraces grown alongside it. Plant it as a warm-season direct-sown melon with full sun and wide spacing, and expect surplus fruit to dry well into the traditional sun-dried melon strips eaten through Uzbek winters.
sources: Mavlyanova, R. et al., 'Melons of Uzbekistan' (Bioversity International / Uzbek Research Institute of Plant Industry, 2005)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring against a warm, sun-baked, sheltered site; Taifi needs an unusually long, hot growing season and resents any real winter cold.

directions: Taifi is an ancient table grape said to have reached Central Asia from the Arabian port city of Taif over a thousand years ago, and it has since become one of Tajikistan's signature grapes, also widely grown in Uzbekistan. Vines carry unusually large, loosely packed conical clusters of big, oval, dark pink berries covered in a waxy bloom, prized for a sweet flavor that local growers and tasters rate well above the same variety grown in cooler regions. It demands an exceptionally long, hot growing season to ripen fully and has very weak cold tolerance, so it is only practical in warm, mild-winter climates, though it otherwise shrugs off the salty, drought-prone soils common in its homeland. Train vines on a sturdy trellis in full sun, water deeply but infrequently once established, and expect this to be a late-season grape that rewards patience with excellent keeping quality after harvest.
